The attacker triggered unauthorized minting on Ethereum and BSC, extracting approximately 52.2 ETH (~$110,000) in value before the MAPO token crashed 96%.

name: Ankr
description: A vulnerability in Ankr’s ankrFLOW liquid-staking contract allowed an attacker to create approximately 8.6M unbacked ankrFLOW. The attacker supplied the unbacked tokens as collateral on MORE Markets and borrowed approximately 15.5M WFLOW from its lending reserve. MORE Markets’ contracts operated as designed; Flow identified the originating vulnerability as Ankr’s ankrFLOW contract

name: Evoq Finance
description: On BNB Chain, Evoq Finance's smart contract was compromised when an attacker stole the owner's private key. The attacker transferred contract ownership, deployed a malicious upgrade, and drained approximately $420K from the protocol and user-approved token accounts.

name: LML/USDT staking protocol
description: On April 1, 2026, the LML/USDT staking protocol on BSC was exploited for $950K via price manipulation. Attacker purchased nearly all LML supply from PancakeSwap using 309.5M USDT, burned tokens, and manipulated TWAP to claim rewards at artificially inflated rates, causing LML to crash 99.6% to $0.1758.

name: BounceBit
description: BounceBit Chain was exploited through an authorization flaw in a protocol-level module inherited from the Evmos stack. A function supporting vesting/lockup operations allowed the caller to specify another account as the source of funds without correctly verifying that the source account had authorized the debit. The attacker used this flaw to transfer 286.54M BB from nine accounts without stealing private keys or forging signatures. BounceBit subsequently halted the chain and decided to retire its Layer 1 and reissue BB on BNB Chain from a pre-exploit snapshot

name: Drop
description: Neutron governance proposal 9 reassigned administration of Drop’s dATOM converter and withdrawal-manager contracts to the attacker. After the proposal passed, the attacker migrated both contracts to previously uploaded malicious code exposing a withdraw_all function and swept their entire balances. Drop’s liquid-staking or redemption logic itself was not exploited; the contracts were taken over through Neutron chain governance

name: Ledger (Supply Chain)
description: Attackers purchased genuine Ledger hardware wallets, installed concealed components capable of capturing recovery phrases, and redistributed the modified devices through resellers. The implants monitored the wallets’ displays during initialization and transmitted captured recovery phrases through cellular connections. Attackers subsequently derived users’ private keys and drained their cryptocurrency holdings. Ledger confirmed that its Secure Element, operating system, and internal infrastructure were not compromised

name: New Gold Protocol
description: New Gold Protocol (NGP) was exploited on its launch day when the attacker exploited a flashloan-powered price oracle manipulation. The protocol relied on DEX pair reserves to calculate the NGP token price, allowing a single Uniswap pool to be manipulated. The attacker used a flash loan to distort pool balances, artifically lowering the reported price to bypass transaction limits and acquire massive amounts of tokens at unrealistic prices. Stolen assets were bridged to Ethereum through Tornado Cash.

name: IPOR Fusion
description: On January 6, 2026, Fusion PlasmaVault on Arbitrum was exploited via EIP-7702 delegation; missing instantWithdraw validation allowed malicious fuse contracts to execute arbitrary code and drain $336K USDC. ~$267K was moved to Tornado Cash.

name: Volo Vault
description: On April 21, 2026, Volo Protocol on Sui was exploited when a high-privilege admin key was compromised, likely via social engineering. The attacker drained three vaults: WBTC (~$2.1M), XAUm (~$0.9M), and USDC (~$0.5M). The team recovered ~$3.44M (90%) of funds after blocking a $500K bridge attempt.

name: Hyperliquid Malaysia
description: On August 6, 2026, a wallet associated with Hyperliquid Malaysia was exploited via a compromised private key on Solana. The exploiter address was identified on-chain; the loss amount was not disclosed and no dedicated post-mortem has been published.

name: DEXX
description: On November 16, 2024, DEXX memecoin trading terminal suffered a security breach affecting at least 900 users when attackers gained access to private keys and drained wallet contents across Solana. Post-investigation estimates reached $30M, with SlowMist linking 8,620+ wallets to the attacker and one user losing over $1M.

name: Bizness
description: Standing on Bizness protocol on Base was exploited via a reentrancy vulnerability in its contract logic. The attacker repeatedly called functions before state was properly updated, enabling them to drain funds through reentrant calls.

name: Sorra Finance
description: Sorra Finance's staking contract had a critical flaw in the getPendingRewards() function that failed to track and deduct previously claimed rewards. The attacker deposited 122,868 SOR tokens with a 14-day lockup, then repeatedly called withdraw() to claim the same rewards multiple times before the state was updated.

name: Dexodus Finance
description: On May 26, 2025, Dexodus Finance's leverage module was exploited for ~$291K via a stale Chainlink oracle report. The attacker used the valid but outdated data to enter a 100x leveraged long position at artificially low ETH price, then closed at the correct price within the same transaction. Dexodus recovered 100% of affected liquidity within 24 hours.

name: BSC TMM/USDT
description: On April 4, 2026, attacker used flashloans to burn ~850M TMM tokens, reducing the TMM reserve to 1 token in the TMM/USDT pool. This price distortion allowed swapping for 272M USDT, netting $1.665M profit after flashloan repayment. Inadequate access controls enabled the large-scale burn.

name: Cyrus Finance
description: On March 22, 2026, Cyrus Finance on BSC was exploited through price manipulation. Attacker abused reliance on live PancakeSwap V3 spot price in withdrawal logic, with no TWAP or oracle resistance, to extract liquidity and tokens.

name: SIR
description: On March 30, 2025, SIR.trading on Ethereum was exploited for $355K via callback validation flaw. Vault contract's callback did not validate Uniswap pool address, allowing replacement with attacker-controlled address via transient storage manipulation (one of first Dencun-targeted exploits).

name: Yearn Finance
description: Yearn Finance's legacy V1 TUSD vault was exploited for $300K via a donation attack. Attackers deposited Fulcrum sUSD tokens to artificially inflate share price, allowing Yearn TUSD tokens to be minted at minimal cost before the price collapsed.

name: Raydium AMM
description: Raydium on Solana lost $1.34M on June 10, 2026 in its deprecated AMM V3 program when attacker bypassed LP token validation using a fake token address. Attacker drained inactive pools containing USDC, SOL and RAY by bypassing proportion checks.

name: RRWallet
description: On August 6, 2026, RRWallet was exploited via weak key generation on Bitcoin, allowing an attacker to derive private keys and steal approximately $2,000,000. Flagged by Coinspect; no dedicated post-mortem has been published.

name: Ambient
description: An attacker exploited Ambient Finance's single-contract architecture by transferring 50 ETH to a newly created contract and extracting ~83.72 ETH via insufficient access controls in the deposit/withdrawal logic.

name: Flamincome
description: Flamincome’s VaultYUSDT strategy valued its Convex-staked Curve USDP LP position using the strategy’s BaseRewardPool.balanceOf() multiplied by Curve’s spot get_virtual_price(). The attacker used approximately $18M USDT of Morpho flash liquidity to acquire USDP and imbalance-mint USDP metapool LP, then permissionlessly staked LP for the strategy through Convex. This temporarily increased the strategy’s reported holdings/NAV. VaultYUSDT immediately incorporated the manipulated valuation into its share price, allowing the attacker to redeem shares at an inflated value and force the strategy to withdraw real aUSDT liquidity from Aave

name: Keplr Wallet (Web3Auth)
description: In November 2026, attackers conducted unauthorized transactions from Keplr wallets created using Google or Apple social login, affecting accounts that relied on Web3Auth's third-party authentication and key-management infrastructure. Keplr and Web3Auth launched a joint investigation and suspended affected login services. Wallets created using recovery phrases or hardware wallets were not believed to be affected. The exact vulnerability, total funds stolen, and affected blockchain networks remained undisclosed

name: Truebit
description: Truebit Protocol suffered $26.44M exploit on January 8, 2026 from integer overflow in token purchase logic (Solidity 0.6.10 unpatched). Attacker minted TRU at negligible cost and sold to bonding-curve for ~$26M; TRU crashed 99.9%.

name: The Idols
description: The Idols NFT contract had a flaw in the _beforeTokenTransfer function that incorrectly handled reward distribution when sender and recipient were the same address. By repeatedly calling safeTransferFrom with identical from/to addresses, an attacker exploited the logic flaw to drain 97 stETH from the reward pool.

name: Affluent
description: Affluent’s lending vaults reportedly suffered unauthorized share minting that allowed attackers to redeem vault assets without providing corresponding deposits. The supplied analysis identifies suspicious transactions on September 30, October 12, and October 16, 2026, involving multiple wallets. Extracted assets were reportedly transferred through exchanges, swaps, and cross-chain services

name: BigONE
description: On July 16, 2025, BigONE crypto exchange suffered a supply chain attack where an attacker gained access to production infrastructure and modified critical backend logic to automatically approve fraudulent withdrawal requests. The attack drained approximately $27 million across five blockchains before being detected.

name: Ethervista
description: EtherVista’s EtherVistaPair.swap() contained an integer overflow vulnerability in its constant-product invariant check. Because the contract multiplied two uint112 reserves without sufficient overflow protection, the calculation could wrap around and incorrectly validate swaps that reduced the pool’s actual reserve product. An attacker registered a malicious contract as an authorized router and executed two crafted swaps to withdraw WETH and VISTA from the pool

name: Meter
description: On September 23 at 21:14 UTC, an attacker exploited a block-validation flaw on Meter mainnet that allowed unbacked MTR and MTRG to be created. The attacker dumped the counterfeit assets through DEXs and bridged proceeds out of Meter. Meter paused both mainnet and its bridge and warned that transactions after block 100731417 may not be honored. The team preserved chain state and is determining a recovery method

name: Thetanuts Finance
description: A deprecated Thetanuts Finance Index Vault was exploited through an integer-division rounding flaw in its mint accounting. Using a flash loan, the attacker reduced the index token supply to a minimal level and repeatedly minted replacement shares while required underlying-token deposits rounded to zero, allowing the attacker to retain assets redeemed from the vault. The attacker extracted 105,471.499078 USDC plus residual option-token positions. About one hour later, a whitehat used the same vulnerability to secure approximately $2M of assets from another vulnerable legacy vault

name: ZKSwap
description: On July 9, 2025, ZKSwap's Ethereum Layer 1 bridge was exploited through its emergency withdrawal mechanism (Exodus Mode). The attacker exploited a critical flaw where the verifyExitProof() function failed to perform actual cryptographic verification of zero-knowledge proofs. By forging withdrawal proofs, the attacker artificially inflated their balance and withdrew approximately $5 million in assets.

name: Movie Token
description: Movie Token's extractFromPoolForLpMining function burned tokens directly from the PancakeSwap MT/WBNB LP pair without the pair's knowledge. Combined with a flash swap callback, this allowed the attacker to collapse the pool's MT reserve from 6.76M to 21K, enabling massive sell orders at inflated prices.

name: X100
description: X100’s governance system allowed an attacker to obtain two of three Senate seats using flash-loan-funded X tokens. The attacker immediately used this majority to approve and execute a malicious treasury proposal within the same transaction. The proposal forced the Freezer to swap 400,000 X tokens into an attacker-controlled liquidity pool with zero minimum output, allowing the attacker to extract treasury value through a manipulated trade

name: Wemix
description: An attacker stole authentication credentials for Wemix's Nile NFT platform service monitoring system and used them to gain access to the Play Bridge Vault. The attacker executed 13 successful withdrawals over two months of preparation, extracting 8.65 million WEMIX tokens and selling them on external exchanges. Wemix delayed disclosure by one week citing precautionary measures.

name: Dango
description: On April 13, 2026, Dango Protocol was exploited for $1.9M via missing validation on donation amounts. Attackers donated negative amounts to manipulate protocol balances, cashing out $410K before the team recovered $1.49M in tokens.

name: Ravencoin
description: On August 7, 2026, the Ravencoin network was affected by a missing input validation issue. Flagged by the Ravencoin project; the loss amount was not disclosed and no dedicated post-mortem has been published.

name: BBXToken
description: BBXToken's transfer function includes a burn mechanism that transfers liquidity pool tokens to a dead address before calling sync(). An attacker exploited this to artificially manipulate PancakeSwap's pool reserves, creating an imbalance that allowed extraction of value from the pool.

name: Echo Bridge
description: Echo Protocol's Monad bridge was compromised on May 18, 2026 when attacker obtained admin key with minting privileges, minting 1,000 eBTC and executing swaps to extract 385 ETH (~$821K realized).

name: Aethir
description: On April 9, 2026, attacker took over AethirOFTAdapter on BNB Chain and drained ~423K ATH via unprotected ownership/admin function with no multisig or timelock. Funds were bridged to TRON via Symbiosis; Aethir disconnected contracts and coordinated blacklisting with major exchanges.

name: Qubic
description: An attacker exploited predictable wallet seeds generated with insufficient randomness in Qubic’s wallet software, compromising 1,404 user wallets and stealing approximately 2.94 trillion QU. The vulnerability affected certain wallets created on Apple devices and Safari browsers. Qubic halted its network at tick 85,371,949, while MEXC froze the account receiving the remaining stolen funds. Seed generation was corrected in wallet version 4.26.4

name: MANTRA Chain
description: MANTRA Chain halted its network after detecting an exploit involving its Cosmos EVM module. The incident was isolated to two MANTRA-controlled wallets and was traced to a vulnerability in an upstream dependency. MANTRA contained the immediate threat, prepared a patched release, and stated that no user funds were exploited

name: Matez
description: On November 21, 2024, the Matez protocol on BNB Chain was exploited via an integer truncation vulnerability in its arithmetic operations, resulting in approximately $80K in losses.

name: Dominion
description: An attacker exploited Dominion’s treasury wallet associated with SILV, Dominion’s tokenized silver product on Solana. Sunrise confirmed the incident originated with Dominion and was not a compromise of Sunrise infrastructure. Sunrise subsequently removed the SILV market from its UI and warned users not to interact with the SILV token while Dominion and its security partners investigate. The exact mechanism through which the treasury wallet was compromised has not yet been disclosed

name: TrustedVolumes
description: An attacker exploited missing access control in TrustedVolumes' RFQ swap proxy to add themselves to the order signer allowlist, forge trade orders, and drain funds across 85 transactions in WETH, WBTC, USDT, and USDC.

name: YieldCore-3rd-deal
description: YieldCore's RWAVault overrode ERC4626 withdraw() and redeem() functions but removed the standard authorization check when msg.sender ≠ owner. Any caller could specify an arbitrary depositor as owner and direct withdrawn assets to an arbitrary receiver. An attacker drained 392,764 USDC of principal from eight depositors across multiple calls.

name: dTRINITY dLEND
description: On March 17, 2026, dTRINITY dLEND was exploited for ~$257K through an empty market vulnerability. The attacker manipulated the liquidityIndex via repeated flashloan premium accrual on a newly-deployed cbBTC reserve with near-zero liquidity, inflating collateral valuations and enabling borrowing of the entire dUSD supply.

name: Ionic Protocol
description: Attackers impersonated Lombard Finance members to trick Ionic Money into listing counterfeit LBTC. Attackers then minted 250 fake LBTC as collateral to borrow $8.6-8.8M in legitimate tokens, bridging ~$3.5M to Ethereum. Inadequate identity verification enabled the social engineering.

name: Veil Cash
description: On February 20-21, 2026, Veil Cash on Base was exploited for 2.9 ETH (~$5.7K). Attacker exploited a misconfigured Groth16 SNARK verifier with identical delta and gamma parameters, breaking the soundness equation and enabling proof forgery to withdraw 29 times from the privacy pool without depositing.

name: 1inch Swap
description: On March 5, 2025, 1inch disclosed a $5M exploit in Fusion v1 resolver contracts when a buffer overflow in _settleOrder() allowed an attacker to trigger integer underflow and hijack control flow to impersonate resolvers and execute unauthorized swaps. Most funds were recovered after negotiation.

name: Unleash Protocol
description: On December 30, 2025, Unleash Protocol was exploited when an attacker compromised the multisig governance system and deployed a malicious contract. The attacker siphoned $3.9M in assets, bridged them to Ethereum, and laundered them via Tornado Cash.

name: Verus-Ethereum Bridge
description: On July 23, 2026 (second of two exploits in 66 days), Verus-Ethereum Bridge was drained of $7.54M via the import path; a small 0.01 VRSC transaction triggered unbacked ETH/tBTC payouts due to missing deposit verification. The vulnerability repeated from May and was never patched.

name: Hyperbridge
description: On April 13, 2026, Hyperbridge's Token Gateway was exploited via unbound Merkle proof verification and a zero-second challenge period. Attacker forged a cross-chain message, minted 1 billion bridged DOT, and liquidated for approximately $2.5M in ETH and incentive pool losses; funds traced to Binance and partially frozen.

name: Swell
description: An attacker gained control of approximately 30 Swell operational keys across multiple networks, including the swETH/rswETH oracle bot. The attacker drained wallet balances, artificially increased swETH and rswETH exchange rates by submitting unbacked reserve values, and redirected EigenLayer reward claims. They also deployed malicious upgrade contracts capable of draining approximately 2,513 ETH, although these upgrades had not been approved or executed when the investigation was published

name: BitoPro
description: BitoPro exchange hot wallets compromised through malware deployment on a cloud operations team member via social engineering. Unauthorized withdrawals executed across multiple blockchains during a system update. Attackers attributed to North Korean Lazarus group based on attack patterns and methodology.

name: IoTeX
description: On February 21, 2026, ioTube bridge's Ethereum-side Validator contract private key was compromised via social engineering targeting an employee. The attacker performed a malicious upgrade bypassing validation and signature checks, gaining control of TokenSafe and MintPool. Approximately $4.3M in USDC, USDT, IOTX, WBTC, and BUSD were drained within hours. Attackers were credited to the same group behind the Infini exploit.

name: AFX Bridge
description: On July 22, 2026, AFX Trade's Arbitrum bridge was exploited when the attacker obtained 5 of 7 validator private keys, bypassing the 2/3 multisig threshold and draining $24.15M in USDC. The attacker converted funds to ETH and consolidated them in a single wallet. AFX offered a 30% bounty for fund recovery.

name: SKP
description: An attacker exploited SKP's transfer hook that called pair.sync() prematurely during token transfers, before the router completed the corresponding swap. This allowed the attacker to manipulate reserve ratios mid-transaction by calling sync() from inside the transfer flow. The attacker assembled $204M in capital from flash loan sources and nearly completely drained the SKP/USDT pair, extracting $212K.

name: BitMart
description: On November 2, 2026, attackers breached BitMart and transferred approximately $391,000 in cryptocurrency from exchange-associated wallets on Base, Arbitrum, and Optimism. Blockchain investigators traced portions of the stolen funds to addresses associated with the Mercado Bitcoin exploit, which occurred on the same day. BitMart founder Sheldon Xia confirmed the breach and said the exchange had investigated the incident and strengthened its security measures. The initial access method remains unidentified

name: WUSD.fi/Glove
description: WUSD.fi's GLOVE reward system lacked Sybil protection. On May 25, 2026, attackers created Sybil wallets and used flashloans to repeatedly collect rewards, draining ~$200K from Uniswap V3.

name: DGLD
description: DGLD (gold-backed stablecoin) cross-chain bridge on Base was exploited on February 23, 2026. Attackers discovered they could mint over 100M unbacked DGLD tokens on Base within 2.5 hours, where legitimate circulation was ~70.8M. Economic impact was ~$250,000, absorbed by DGLD as the primary liquidity provider.

name: Cozy V2
description: Cozy Finance lost $427K on August 29, 2025 on Optimism when completeWithdraw function lacked caller verification, letting attacker complete withdrawals using only a user's redemption ID.

name: zkLend
description: zkLend lost $9.57M on February 11, 2025 on Starknet via an integer division rounding vulnerability. Attacker exploited truncated rounding in withdrawal calculations with precise wstETH deposits to inflate their raw_balance to 1724, draining all tokens from other pools. Attacker returned ~$3.2M after negotiation but lost remaining to a Tornado Cash scam.

name: 402bridge
description: On October 27, 2025, 402bridge on Base was compromised just days after mainnet launch, affecting over 200 users and losing 17,693 USDC. Attackers accessed private keys stored on servers with excessive authorization permissions in the x402 mechanism.

name: TSR
description: On June 1, 2026 TesseraDAO's mint function was exploited via inadequate access control, allowing an attacker to mint approximately 99 million TSR tokens, immediately selling them on PancakeSwap for ~2.5M USDT, then bridging to Ethereum and laundering funds via Tornado Cash.

name: BTCPay Server
description: On November 1, 2026, attackers exploited a vulnerability in BTCPay Server versions 2.4.1 and earlier to compromise self-hosted installations and steal BTC and LTC from their hot wallets. The vulnerability had been patched in version 2.4.2 in August, but outdated installations remained exposed. BTCPay Server urged affected operators to take their servers offline, migrate to fresh installations, replace compromised wallet seeds, and rotate potentially exposed credentials. Wallets whose spending keys were held off-server, including hardware wallets, were unaffected

name: Arrakis V1
description: The attacker flash-loaned 1,800 WETH and swapped approximately 145 WETH for ENS to manipulate the ENS/WETH Uniswap V3 pool’s instantaneous spot price. The Arrakis V1 vault used pool.slot0() to value its Uniswap V3 position during mint() and burn() without a TWAP or price-deviation guard. The attacker minted vault shares while the price was distorted, restored the pool price, then burned the shares for a more valuable token mix, resulting in approximately 2.94 WETH profit

name: SUPERFORTUNE AI
description: An attacker exploited insufficient verification controls in the multisig transaction process to redirect an airdrop transfer. A lookalike address was substituted for the GUA token claim contract, allowing the attacker to intercept the transfer.

name: SQ Protocol
description: SQ Protocol was exploited when an attacker used EIP-7702 authorized transactions to call privileged staking functions via a hardcoded owner backdoor, minting fake positions and draining USDT.

name: Goldfinch
description: A flaw in Goldfinch's legacy collectInterestRepayment() function permitted transfers from any approved address without proper safeguards. An attacker deposited USDC to manipulate share price, then repeatedly withdrew inflated amounts, draining the victim's holdings through the contract's misconfigured approval logic.

name: ElevateFi
description: An attacker manipulated the EFI/DAI Uniswap V2 pair's spot price mid-transaction using flash-loan-funded buying pressure, then exploited ElevateFi's staking vault which relied on raw pair reserves without any time-weighted or external oracle guard. By inflating EFI's spot price during staking, the attacker received disproportionate staking positions: creating $2.5M recorded staking principal for only 713.5 EFI of actual principal, repeated 100 times.

name: DxSale
description: Attacker exploited unprotected owner key in DxSale's legacy 2021 locker contract on May 26-27, 2026, draining over 1,400 liquidity pools on BNB Chain for $7.3M using EIP-7702 batch delegation. Key had no timelocks or multisig controls.

name: Little Boy Plus
description: On June 17, 2026, Little Boy Plus was exploited for ~$377.6K USDT when a zero-value transferFrom call bypassed authorization checks in the custom transfer logic. This enabled the attacker to mint LBP tokens directly into the PancakeSwap pair, creating a reserve imbalance exploitable via swap.

name: GoonFi
description: GoonFi v2's WSOL/USDC pool on Solana was drained of ~$254,000 in March 2026 via a program configuration bug in the AMM pricing logic.

name: Ajna V2
description: Attackers exploited Ajna’s internal liquidation accounting across multiple lending pools. Current on-chain analysis shows liquidation operations could be sequenced to extract collateral while returning insufficient quote assets to the pool, including bucketTake, collateral removal, take, and settlement operations

name: THORChain DEX
description: On May 15, 2026, a flaw in the GG20 threshold-signature scheme securing Asgard vaults allowed a newly churned malicious node to authorize unauthorized withdrawals, draining approximately $10.7-$10.8 million across Bitcoin, Ethereum, BNB Chain, and Base.

name: Tectonic
description: Unverified incident claimed for November 18, 2024 on Cronos chain; extensive search found no credible reports, announcements, or news coverage of a Tectonic hack on this date.

name: Goose Finance
description: Goose Finance on BSC exploited for $8K via share accounting flaw in vault withdrawal logic on March 14, 2026. The bug evaded prior audits.

name: Hacken Token
description: Hacken's HAI token private key was exposed during bridge architecture changes on Ethereum and BNB Chain. The compromised key allowed minting of 900 million HAI tokens, which were dumped on decentralized exchanges, causing the token price to crash 99%.

name: OlaXBT
description: In September 2025 OlaXBT suffered a multisig wallet compromise resulting in the theft of 32 million AIO tokens (valued at approximately $2 million). The team responded by deploying a new token contract and migrating user holdings.

name: Astera.fi
description: On October 9, 2025, Astera's lending markets on Linea were exploited through a liquidity-index inflation attack. The attacker inflated the index to overvalue their collateral, then borrowed across asUSD, LINEA, and WETH minipools for ~8% of the protocol's TVL. Linea's security team detected the pattern and froze the attack within minutes.

name: Meta Pool
description: On June 17, 2025, Meta Pool's ERC4626 vault contract on Ethereum was exploited via an unprotected mint() function in Staking.sol. An attacker called the public mint function to create 9,705 mpETH tokens (~$27M at face value) without depositing collateral, extracting only $130K due to low liquidity in affected pools.

name: LND
description: LND, a Sonic-based Aave fork, lost $1.18M in May 2025 when a developer with unilateral deployment control introduced a malicious access-control modification that reached production unreviewed. Halborn identified the developer as a DPRK IT worker.

name: ZEROBASE
description: Attackers deployed a malicious phishing contract on BSC that impersonated the ZEROBASE frontend, tricking users into authorizing USDT transfers. The fake contract collected token approvals, then drained hundreds of connected wallets of approximately $250K total, with one user losing $123K.

name: MFT
description: On November 17, 2024, the MFT protocol on BNB Chain was exploited via a logic flaw in its contract implementation, resulting in approximately $33.7K in losses.

name: Alephium Bridge
description: On May 30, 2026, Alephium TokenBridge was exploited via off-chain backend flaw in guardian message verification. Attackers deployed fake contracts to forge VAAs, disrupted node connectivity to trigger fallback validation, and authorized transfers totaling $815K across Ethereum and BNB Chain, plus 13.76M unbacked ALPH minting.

name: RANT
description: On July 5, 2025, RANT token on Binance Smart Chain was exploited through a vulnerability in the _sellBurnLiquidityPairTokens() function. The flaw allowed attackers to manipulate the token burn process and steal approximately $204,000 from the protocol.

name: FutureSwap
description: In December 2025, attacker exploited FutureSwap on Arbitrum using flash loans to acquire temporary governance voting power and pass a malicious proposal transferring protocol funds.

name: Lixir Finance
description: On June 25, 2026, Lixir Finance vaults were exploited via insufficient nonce validation in permit() function. Attacker reused a single non-owner signature across 41 calls on six vault clones to gain allowances and extract USDC, USDT, ETH, and LIX tokens.

name: SwissBorg
description: SwissBorg's SOL Earn program lost 192,600 SOL (~$41.5M) when staking partner Kiln's API credentials were compromised. Attacker embedded malicious authorization instructions in unstaking transactions to transfer withdrawal authority to attacker-controlled addresses.

name: 0G Labs
description: 0G Labs emergencyWithdraw function had improper access control or validation, allowing unauthorized withdrawals of $516K.

name: Reddio RedSonic
description: RedSonic’s permissionless registerErc20() allowed stETH to be registered as a separate vault asset even though the ETH vault’s rsvETH share price already counted the vault’s raw stETH balance through its Lido position. As a result, the same stETH balance simultaneously backed rsvETH and newly minted rsvstETH shares. The attacker deposited stETH to inflate the rsvETH share price, redeemed rsvETH against that inflated valuation, then redeemed rsvstETH to recover the same stETH collateral, effectively using one asset balance to support two share classes

name: Demex Perp
description: Demex’s bridge was exploited through insufficient verification between its bridge module and external-chain contract system. The attacker used a helper contract to falsify token-deployment reports, registering the low-value nLEND token against canonical WETH and WBNB contracts. Subsequent withdrawals released approximately $191,929 in bridge reserves despite deducting only $10.47 worth of nLEND. The withdrawal limiter also failed because it valued the deducted tokens rather than the assets released

name: Meteora DAMM V2
description: On January 17, 2026, Meteora DAMM V2 lost $1.5M when the team transferred funds to a fraudulent OTC counterparty impersonating a legitimate token buyer on Solana, which never delivered tokens.

name: Bankroll Network
description: On June 19, 2025, old BankrollStack contracts containing an integer underflow vulnerability in the sell() function were exploited. Attackers manipulated dividend accounting through lingering token approvals, draining funds from users who had previously interacted with the abandoned contracts.

name: Ribbon
description: Aevo's legacy Ribbon DOV vaults were drained of $2.7 million on December 12, 2025. An oracle upgrade created a decimal mismatch (8 vs 18 decimals) with legacy assets. The attacker exploited a publicly-accessible oracle price-setting function and minimal collateral requirements to create undercollateralized positions and drain the vaults.

name: FlashTrade
description: Flash Trade's Solana perpetuals exchange suffered a $98K unauthorized withdrawal when an attacker exploited an incomplete validation path in MagicBlock's SDK. The ephemeral macro's undelegation callback failed to validate a fake account, allowing the attacker to trigger a fake withdrawal.

name: Radix
description: A Radix Engine execution-layer flaw allowed transactions to obtain direct references to arbitrary internal fungible and non-fungible vaults without verifying that the caller owned or was authorized to access them. The attacker supplied internal vault addresses to custom code and directly invoked withdrawal functionality, bypassing the authorization rules of the accounts and components holding those vaults. Across 26 transactions, the attacker drained nearly the entire Radix supply of six Hyperlane-wrapped assets and then used their normal Hyperlane Warp Routes to bridge the stolen assets out of Radix

name: Impermax V3
description: On November 11, 2025, Impermax V3 on Base suffered a $380K exploit. The attacker created tiny positions in low-liquidity cbBTC-tBTC pairs to push totalBalance toward zero, collapsing the exchange rate and enabling exponential minting of borrowable tokens. When totalBalance hit zero, all deposits were redirected to the attacker.

name: DeltaPrime
description: On November 11, 2024, DeltaPrime was exploited across Arbitrum and Avalanche when an attacker created a malicious trading pair, used it to convert borrowed collateral into fake reward tokens, and withdrew them, leaving the protocol with ~$4.8M in uncollateralized bad debt. This was DeltaPrime's second major hack in 2024.

name: AlpsCon AI Trade Hub
description: AlpsCon AI Trade Hub’s V7–V9 contracts incorrectly applied accumulated historical profit-per-share values to balances imported from preceding versions, allowing newly deposited funds to claim rewards accrued before the deposits existed. The attacker used a flash loan to create temporary ALPS service credits and exploited the accounting flaw to extract USDC. The attack was facilitated by an authorization whitelist containing a publicly known Hardhat test account, which the attacker used through EIP-7702 delegation

name: Makina
description: An attacker took a $280M flashloan and used $170M to manipulate Makina's sharePrice oracle via three compounding flaws: permissionless oracle updates, synchronous Curve spot prices with no TWAP, and pre-approved Weiroll paths. Extracted ~$4.2M.

name: Token of Power
description: Attacker acquired >50% voting power of TOP token via Balancer pool and passed malicious governance proposal to mint massive tokens, draining $1.58M WETH from Balancer V1 pool. Vulnerability stemmed from extremely low token supply (16,384 TOP total).

name: Astra Nova
description: Astra Nova's RVV token launch was disrupted when a third-party market maker account was compromised. The attacker gained access and liquidated 8.6% of the token supply for approximately $10.2M in USDT, causing the token price to plummet 75%. The attacker held stolen funds in USDT on a centralized exchange, allowing the team to coordinate recovery efforts.

name: JHY Token
description: JHY Token's TokenDividendTracker contract had a critical flaw where it set user balances to the LP token balance, allowing users to swap more tokens than they owned. This accounting error enabled attackers to drain funds by exploiting the incorrect balance tracking.

name: CrowdRingCircle
description: CrowdRingCircle's token contract allowed the pair's recorded reserves to desynchronize with actual balances by burning CRC directly from the pair address before calling sync(). An attacker exploited this to artificially inflate CRC's price and drain USDT from the PancakeSwap V2 CRC/USDT pool.

name: SlurpyCoin
description: SlurpyCoin was exploited via a flash loan attack that targeted its buyback mechanism. The attacker used sandwiched swaps to manipulate price and profit from the deflationary token's burning logic.

name: Float Protocol
description: The attacker used flash-loan-funded swaps to manipulate the Uniswap V3 pool’s slot0 spot price consumed by Float’s Hypervisor contracts. This distorted currentTick() / getTotalAmounts() and consequently the valuation of LP shares, allowing the attacker to repeatedly deposit and withdraw at manipulated share values and extract 10.71 ETH

name: SecondFi
description: Between June 21-23, 2026, deterministic nonce reuse in SecondFi's Cardano signing code (one missing line) exposed 374 wallet private keys through all historical signatures. Attacker drained 16.1M ADA (~$2.4M); white hat protected $18.5M ADA. Total exposure: $20M+.

name: Bitmor
description: In May 2026, Bitmor DCA contract on Base was exploited; access control flaw allowed attackers to drain wallets of any users with active token approvals.

name: Solido Cash
description: On July 23, 2026, Solido Cash's CDP suffered an oracle attack when the SOLID price feed went stale and fell back to near-par CASH valuation (0.99919999) while SOLID was trading at 22.2 SUPRA per unit. An attacker looped acquire-collateral, mint-CASH, sell-CASH twice across 18:21 UTC and 21:12 UTC transactions, minting 809,052 CASH of unbacked debt and selling it for 293.7M SUPRA.

name: Custom sAVAX Rebalancer
description: On April 19, 2026, a custom rebalancer contract on Avalanche was exploited via an arbitrary external call vulnerability. The attacker abused a public function that executed unchecked external calls while the contract held delegated credit from Aave V3, allowing them to borrow WAVAX on behalf of victims and extract approximately $64K.

name: Balancer V1
description: An attacker first used swaps to reduce the Balancer V1 BPool’s WBTC reserve to near-dust levels, then exploited rounding in joinswapPoolAmountOut. When the function reverse-calculated the WBTC required to mint a caller-specified amount of BPT, 18-decimal fixed-point arithmetic rounded the required input down to 1 satoshi while still minting the full BPT amount. The attacker minted 4,408.8 BPT through these underpriced joins and exited the pool proportionally to drain DPI, USDC, WETH, and WBTC

name: Bitcoin Mission
description: Bitcoin Mission lost ~$1.3M in wrapped BTC in April 2025 when a privileged wrapped BTC handling function lacked access-control checks, allowing an unauthorized caller to move the protocol's holdings.

name: Ekubo
description: On May 5, 2026, Ekubo's EVM swap router contracts were exploited when attackers discovered the contracts failed to verify whether the payer had authorized transactions. Attackers stole 17 wBTC ($1.4 million) and laundered funds via Tornado Cash.

name: Axelar Secret IBC Bridge
description: An attacker exploited the Axelar Secret bridge ics20-for-axelar contract to mint $4.67M of unbacked saTokens by forging IBC deposit packets from a malicious blockchain. The attacker created a minimal Cosmos blockchain with a single validator, opened a fake IBC channel to Secret Network, and sent forged deposit packets that bypassed channel validation. The minted tokens were redeemed back over the legitimate IBC channel to drain Axelar's escrow account, remaining undetected for seven days until a failed cross-chain transfer revealed the empty escrow.

name: AK1111
description: On November 23, 2024, the AK1111 contract on BNB Chain was exploited through an access control vulnerability that allowed unauthorized fund extraction of approximately $31.5K.

name: BeatXswap
description: BeatXswap’s LiquidityVestingConvert contract used the live V3 pool slot0() price as its sole BTX pricing source, without a TWAP, deviation limit, or manipulation check. The attacker flash-borrowed BTX, dumped it into the BTX/USDT V3 pool to sharply reduce sqrtPriceX96, then deposited 10,000 USDT and 2,000 USDT into the vulnerable contracts. The manipulated quote caused the contracts to contribute an excessive amount of their own BTX when minting LP positions, allowing the attacker to extract the BTX before reversing the swaps and repaying the flash loans

name: Wise Lending V2
description: Wise Lending V2 suffered a flashloan exploit on Arbitrum and Ethereum with significant losses. The exact attack vector remains unclear from available public sources.

name: Agentic FoF
description: Agentic FoF suffered a security vulnerability that allowed attackers to drain approximately $531K from its vaults. All vaults were subsequently suspended pending an internal investigation, with the Basis vault secured but also halted as a precaution.

name: Phemex
description: On January 23, 2025, Singapore-based exchange Phemex's hot wallets were drained across more than a dozen chains (ETH, SOL, XRP, BTC, BSC, Tron) in a coordinated attack, with reported losses ranging from $69.1M to $85M. The hot wallet private keys and signing infrastructure were compromised.

name: Silo V2
description: Silo's soUSDC vault was exploited through an immutable oracle that priced wstUSR at 1.133 while market price had collapsed to 0.12, combined with accounting flaws that didn't mint shares for external deposits, allowing attackers to inflate redemption payouts.

name: Polymarket
description: Hackers injected malicious scripts into Polymarket's comment sections, posting phishing links that appeared to offer access to private markets. Users clicking the links were redirected to a fake Polymarket interface where attackers captured their credentials. Over $500K in user funds were drained via compromised email-login accounts.

name: LULA
description: On July 29, 2026, LULA (BEP-20 token on BSC) suffered a ~$578K exploit via business logic flaw. Attacker exploited an accessible recycle() function in the Rental contract to transfer LULA directly from PancakeSwap V2 pair, then manipulated pair reserves via sync() call. Repeated recycle() calls drained LULA reserves to near-zero, allowing small swap for nearly all USDT.

name: BTC24H
description: BTC24H Lock contract on Polygon was exploited in December 2024 for $85,700. The claim function failed to verify if msg.sender was an eligible claimant, allowing anyone to claim BTC24H tokens without authorization.

name: Aventa
description: Aventa Web3 utilities protocol exploited via flash loan attack. The attack mechanism drained approximately 3.9 ETH from the protocol through flashloan-funded exploitation of a protocol vulnerability.

name: Drift Trade
description: On April 1, 2026, Drift Protocol on Solana was exploited for ~$295M when attackers tricked Security Council members into pre-signing transactions via Solana durable nonces, handing over admin control. Attackers whitelisted a worthless fake token (CVT) as collateral, deposited 500M CVT, and withdrew $285M in real assets (USDC, SOL, ETH) in ~12 minutes. Security firms linked the attack to DPRK/Lazarus Group.

name: Syndicate
description: On April 29, 2026, a private key leak allowed attackers to maliciously upgrade Syndicate's Commons bridge contracts and drain approximately 18.5M SYND tokens ($330K-$400K) across two networks.

name: HyperVault
description: HyperVault on Hyperliquid L1 conducted a rug pull in late September 2025, draining $3.6M in user funds. Developers falsely claimed audits by Spearbit and Pashov, then disappeared after moving assets through privacy tools.

name: TAC Protocol
description: The TON-TAC bridge lacked code-hash verification on jetton wallets. An attacker deployed a counterfeit USD₮ wallet and sent a fraudulent bridge message to receive unbacked minted TAC tokens, draining legitimate locked assets.

name: DoinGud
description: DoinGud’s acceptOffer settlement logic transferred an offer’s USDC price to the caller without deleting or zeroing the consumed offer record. Unlike cancelOffer, the acceptance path omitted the swap-and-pop cleanup. Missing checks also permitted the offerer to accept their own offer and permitted a zero NFT amount. By using amount=0, the attacker avoided listing cleanup and replayed identical acceptOffer calldata, causing the contract to pay the same offer repeatedly. A flash loan supplied the temporary USDC needed to construct the self-funded offer. Independent reporting likewise describes the exploit as failure to clear a bid after acceptance

name: b14g
description: On October 31, 2026, an attacker withdrew approximately 97 million CORE from assets staked through b14g and transferred them to attacker-controlled addresses. The protocol paused the affected contracts and coordinated with security partners and exchanges to trace the stolen funds. Approximately 68 million CORE remained on Core, while exchanges froze another 9 million CORE. BTC staked through b14g was unaffected and remained time-locked on Bitcoin

name: Vicuna Lending
description: Vicuna Finance’s S Market and Stablecoin Market were exploited through an oracle manipulation vulnerability, resulting in approximately $700K in losses. The Main Protocol market was unaffected. Following the exploit, Vicuna removed liquidity from the affected submarkets and planned to distribute the remaining assets pro rata to affected users based on their net supplied positions

name: Singularity Finance
description: Singularity Finance on Base exploited for $413K in April 2026 via misconfigured oracle price validation. Attacker manipulated DEX pairs to inflate collateral values.

name: BtcTurk
description: In August 2025, Turkish CEX BtcTurk suffered a second major hack, with $48M drained from hot wallets across 7 blockchains (Ethereum, Avalanche, Arbitrum, Base, Optimism, Mantle, Polygon) after private keys were compromised.

name: Berally
description: On March 14, 2025, Berally on Berachain suffered a hack when the deployer key was compromised, allowing the attacker to drain all vesting tokens from the liquidity pool. The core dApp contracts remained unaffected.

name: Aave V3
description: Aave V3 oracle misconfiguration on March 10-12, 2026 caused ~$862K in losses. Chaos Labs' CAPO system reported wstETH at 1.1939 instead of 1.228, triggering liquidations of 34 otherwise-healthy E-Mode positions due to inconsistent snapshot configuration.

name: WEMIX.FI Lend
description: On July 26, 2026, an attacker obtained administrative control of the WEMIX$ stablecoin contract and minted 5.23M counterfeit WEMIX$ tokens. These were swapped for real WEMIX and USDC.e and dispersed across Ethereum and BNB Chain. The total exploit was estimated at $6.25M.

name: Bisq
description: Bisq v1 was exploited via missing validation on negative miner fee values in trade protocol. Modified client allowed attacker to pull value from multisig outputs; ~11 BTC stolen from 10 users. Bisq v2 and Easy unaffected.

name: Astroport
description: Neutron governance proposal 9 contained MsgUpdateAdmin messages that reassigned administration of Astroport contracts despite those contracts previously being administered by Astroport’s own governance contract. After the proposal passed, the attacker migrated Astroport Staking and six Astroport pair contracts to attacker-uploaded code containing a withdraw_all entry point and swept their balances. The attack did not exploit Astroport’s swap or pool logic

name: Hifi Finance
description: An attacker acquired HIFI governance tokens and used four coordinated votes shortly before voting closed to pass a malicious governance proposal. Proposal 21 would upgrade Hifi’s BalanceSheet contract to introduce a function that incorrectly treats existing collateral as untracked funds, allowing it to be transferred to an attacker-controlled Safe. The proposal would also mint 25 million HIFI tokens to the attacker. At the time of reporting, the proposal was queued but had not been executed

name: Revert Lend
description: Revert Lend's Aerodrome Lend vault on Base was exploited on January 29-30, 2026 for $50,101 when missing validation allowed withdrawal of collateral that was still backing an active loan.

name: Coinbase
description: Coinbase's corporate DEX wallet lost $300,000 on August 13, 2025 when MEV bots exploited misconfigured token approvals granted to a 0x protocol swapper contract.

name: Lien
description: On July 23-24, 2026, Lien Finance on Ethereum suffered a $542,000 exploit when an attacker bypassed the burn-before-swap logic in the GeneralizedDotc contract. The attacker minted unbacked bond tokens and swapped them for USDC from OTC pools.

name: Fegex
description: FEG's SmartBridge was drained for ~$1.3M across Ethereum, BSC and Base. The attacker forged Wormhole messages from an unauthorized chain that the relayer accepted as withdrawal requests without verifying the emitter's authority, marking the third major FEG incident.

name: Humanity
description: Humanity Protocol's admin wallets were drained of $32M and 447M H tokens were unauthorized minted after a Humanity Foundation member's private key was compromised.

name: Alkimiya
description: Alkimiya's SilicaPools contract unsafely downcast shares from uint256 to uint128 in the collateralizedMint function. An attacker used a flash loan to manipulate the truncated shares value, causing the contract to believe it had issued fewer shares than it actually had and allowing redemption of more collateral than deposited.

name: ALEX
description: On June 6, 2025, ALEX Protocol suffered an $8.37M exploit. Attacker deployed a malicious token with custom transfer logic, used it to spoof as-contract origin and masquerade as the vault, draining 8.4M STX, 21.85 sBTC, and stablecoins due to failed access control verification.

name: Oraichain
description: On August 8, 2026, the Oraichain network was exploited via an unbacked cross-chain mint, allowing tokens to be minted without matching collateral on the origin chain. Flagged by the Oraichain team; the loss amount was not disclosed and no dedicated post-mortem has been published.

name: RetoSwap
description: RetoSwap (Haveno protocol) on Monero was exploited on June 16-17, 2026 (second incident in 30 days) when dispute resolution logic permitted fund release without proper two-way settlement. Attacker took buy offers, forced arbitration, and released XMR after Bitcoin confirmations without sending BTC.

name: Venus Core Pool
description: On March 29, 2025 Venus Core Pool on zkSync Era suffered a donation attack when an attacker directly transferred tokens to the cToken contract, distorting exchange rates and accumulator calculations and bypassing collateral accounting and supply cap logic, resulting in $902,000 in losses and bad debt.

name: Abracadabra Spell
description: On October 4, 2025 Abracadabra Money on Ethereum suffered a critical exploit of the cook() multi-action function where improper state handling allowed attackers to bypass solvency checks: Action 5 set needsSolvencyCheck=true, but Action 0 reset the CookStatus, enabling under-collateralized borrowing and withdrawal of 1.79 million MIM tokens.

name: Fluid Lending
description: An attacker compromised operational keys used exclusively by Fluid’s Merkle rewards distribution infrastructure. The attacker used these permissions to submit and approve fraudulent reward allocations, allowing them to claim approximately 125,109 FLUID, 51,946 GHO, and a small amount of cbBTC. The incident was isolated to reward distribution contracts and did not compromise Fluid’s core protocol contracts, lending markets, or user deposits

name: Virtue
description: An attacker exploited Switchboard’s IOTA guardian-attestation design to replace the signing keys of all 14 production oracles and submit arbitrary IOTA prices. The attacker first inflated IOTA to $10M, allowing 4.94M unbacked VUSD to be minted against 1.027 IOTA, then crashed the reported price to trigger liquidations of healthy positions. By pre-positioning the freshly minted VUSD in Virtue’s Stability Pool, the attacker captured 16.72M IOTA-equivalent of collateral from the manipulated liquidations

name: Huma
description: Huma Finance's deprecated V1 BaseCreditPool contracts on Polygon were exploited via a credit-lifecycle logic error combined with unrestricted access control. An attacker created Requested credit records through an open requestCredit() path with preApproved=false, then advanced those unapproved records to GoodStanding using an unrestricted refreshAccount() call. The attacker then exploited drawdown() to borrow the pools' residual balances.

name: TUR Staking
description: On March 26, 2026, the TUR staking protocol on BSC was exploited via a spot price manipulation attack. The attacker manipulated the TUR-NOBEL liquidity pool to artificially inflate the spot price, then used this inflated price to trigger oversized reward calculations in the staking contract. The attacker claimed amplified rewards through a referral account and profited approximately $133K by swapping the stolen TUR for USDT.

name: CrossCurve
description: CrossCurve's ReceiverAxelar contract failed to validate message origin, letting attackers forge cross-chain messages. Attackers crafted messages to release tokens without offsetting deposits on other chains, draining $3M across multiple blockchains.

name: Avici
description: A vulnerability in a version of Rain’s Solana card contract used by Avici allowed unauthorized withdrawals from the contract holding users’ card balances. Avici reported that 1,685 users were affected for $500,859.22. The vulnerable contract was subsequently upgraded across all affected programs

name: Bonfire
description: BonfireSwap’s public transfer path accepted a caller-supplied token owner address and passed it as the from address to BONFIRE’s transferFrom without verifying that the caller was that owner or otherwise authorized by the owner. Because BONFIRE saw BonfireSwap itself as msg.sender, existing victim-to-BonfireSwap allowances authorized the transfers. The attacker repeatedly selected wallets with standing approvals, transferred their BONFIRE into the BONFIRE/WBNB PancakeSwap pair, and used the router’s public skim path to collect the resulting excess before selling the harvested BONFIRE for BNB. No private key, admin privilege, flash loan, or PancakeSwap invariant failure was required

name: FlashLoopAdapter
description: FlashLoopAdapter’s open()/close() authorization trusted any caller whose isModuleEnabled() response returned true, allowing an attacker-controlled fake Safe to pass the check. The attacker then supplied each real victim Safe as swapRouter and encoded execTransactionFromModule(...) as arbitrary swapCalldata. Because FlashLoopAdapter was already an enabled module on those Safes, they accepted the calls and transferred or withdrew collateral to the attacker

name: Initia
description: Initia suffered a security incident involving the unauthorized minting of multiple assets on its L1. The attacker reportedly transferred and converted some of the minted assets into Ethereum-based holdings. Initia halted its L1 and rollups while investigating the vulnerability and coordinating with validators, exchanges, and security teams

name: Mure
description: Mure's MureDistribution proxy on Ethereum was drained in a single transaction on 21 May 2026 after a caller-controlled signer address was passed to SignatureChecker, causing it to fall through to the ERC-1271 path and return true for a forged signature. This authorized transferFrom of 4.85M QUEST tokens pre-approved to the proxy, which sold for ~5.45 ETH (~$11.7K).

name: Ploutos Money
description: Ploutos Money oracle misconfigured to use BTC/USD feed for USDC pricing. Attacker borrowed 187 ETH by depositing only 8 USDC (~10^12x discrepancy), exploiting the misconfiguration within one block.

name: Flooring Protocol
description: Flooring Protocol was exploited on June 8, 2026 via a packed storage and token-indexing vulnerability in its DN404/BT404 implementation. Attacker deposited small WETH to mint near-infinite fpToken balances, draining multiple NFT pools. Yuga Labs white hats rescued 68 blue-chip NFTs ($500K+) including 29 BAYC, 4 Mutant Apes and 2 CryptoPunks.

name: Ostium
description: On July 15, 2026, Ostium perpetuals DEX on Arbitrum suffered a $23.75M exploit when an attacker used a compromised price oracle private key to sign fraudulent Bitcoin price reports ($5,000 vs. real ~$60,000), opening positions at fake prices and closing at market rates.

name: INK Finance
description: INK Finance's Workspace Treasury Proxy on Polygon was exploited on May 11, 2026 for $140K USDT. Attacker deployed a malicious contract matching a whitelisted claimer address to bypass authorization checks and trigger unauthorized treasury transfers, facilitated by a $25K flash loan.

name: NFTG
description: On November 26, 2024, the NFTG protocol on BNB Chain suffered an access control vulnerability that allowed unauthorized fund extraction. The vulnerability was in the contract's access controls, permitting unauthorized callers to drain approximately $10K.

name: Clober Liquidity Vault
description: On December 10, 2024, Clober Liquidity Vault on Base was exploited for ~$501K via reentrancy in the Rebalancer contract's _burn function. The attacker used a malicious contract and 267.4 ETH flashloan to execute repeated state reads before balance updates.

name: zkFinance
description: No credible sources found documenting a zkFinance hack on November 11, 2024, or proximate dates on zkSync Era.

name: Aztec Bridge
description: Aztec's private rollup bridge escape-hatch mechanism was exploited via incomplete proof validation, allowing an attacker to manipulate proof data and withdraw 1,158 ETH, 150,000 DAI, and ~0.47 renBTC. This was the second Aztec exploit in June 2026; the June 14 attack drained ~$2.1M via similar proof manipulation.

name: SEA Token
description: Suspicious attack on Arbitrum drained ~$153K from SEA token interactions; suspected price oracle or liquidity manipulation but mechanism unconfirmed pending technical analysis.

name: Moonwell Lending
description: Moonwell Lending on Base suffered a $1.78M loss when AI-generated code misconfigured the cbETH oracle to price it at $1.12 instead of nearly $2,200, failing to multiply the exchange rate by the price feed. This enabled abnormal liquidations and borrowing.

name: Surf Lending
description: A machine with access to Surf Lending’s admin key was compromised. According to Surf’s lead developer, the incident was not caused by a smart-contract bug. Surf placed the protocol into maintenance mode, temporarily migrated user vaults and supplied assets to its multisig treasury wallet, and began migrating the V1 contracts while rebuilding the affected infrastructure in a more secure environment. Surf subsequently described the event as a security incident and prioritized restoring V1

name: Chi Protocol
description: Chi Protocol exploited on July 13, 2026 for ~$8.5K. Attacker flash-loaned 5 WETH, bought depegged USC from a thin Uniswap V2 pool, and burned it against the ReserveHolder. The burn() function assumed a $1 peg without checking, redeeming full-value collateral.

name: Hyperdrive HL Lending
description: On September 27, 2025 Hyperdrive (lending protocol on Hyperliquid L1) lost approximately $782,000 to an exploit where attackers exploited an arbitrary router call vulnerability, making repeated withdrawals from the Primary USDT0 Market and Treasury USDT Market and extracting ~673,000 USDT0 and 110,244 thBILL, with stolen funds bridged to Ethereum ($494k) and BNB Chain ($279k).

name: MAAT Protocol
description: MAAT Protocol's withdrawal logic had a critical edge case where not all shares were burned during withdrawals from the BSC Stargate strategy. This left 1 wei of shares in the contract, allowing third-party addresses to call redeem with minimal share input and drain funds without consuming shares.

name: Bodega Market
description: An attacker exploited a vulnerability in Bodega Market’s prediction-market contracts to drain rewards and market seed funds. The team associated the exploit with a transaction involving an M-EVIL_ORACLE token, but has not yet disclosed the underlying vulnerability or explained how that token enabled the drain. Because the exploit mechanism remains under investigation, the precise root cause is not yet confirmed

name: Edel
description: On June 30, 2026, Edel Finance's xStock lending protocol was exploited via flash loan-enabled oracle manipulation. The attacker manipulated the wGOOGLx (tokenized Google shares) exchange rate, inflating collateral value by ~7,700% due to a missing price oracle fallback, allowing extraction of $403K in bad debt.

name: FilDA
description: An attacker manipulated token pricing used by FilDA’s Glide LP price oracle on Elastos Smart Chain, allowing the attacker to exploit distorted asset valuations and drain more than 140,000 ELA and 5,800 USDC from the lending protocol. FilDA subsequently suspended its ESC deployment and announced that it would permanently shut it down

name: AFI Protocol
description: On 30 May 2026 the afiUSD vault of AFI Protocol, a proof-of-reserve and yield-vault platform for RWAs on Ethereum, was drained of approximately $480,000. AFI paused the affected vault within hours, rotated operational keys across the platform, and reported that its other vaults and the remaining ~$225M TVL were unaffected. The attacker swapped ~$252k DAI to ETH and sent ~150 ETH through Tornado Cash. AFI has not published the exploit path.

name: Transit Finance
description: On May 12, 2026, Transit Finance on Tron was exploited for $1.88M via deprecated contract officially discontinued in 2022 but left active on-chain. Attacker exploited historical vulnerabilities to drain DAI and other assets.

name: Myriad Markets
description: An attacker exploited a previously exposed private key belonging to Myriad’s automated market management wallet. The key had reportedly been leaked through a vulnerability in a third-party library used by a backend service. The attacker used the wallet’s privileges to manipulate positions and force incorrect resolutions across 10 prediction markets on BNB Chain. Myriad revoked the wallet’s permissions, secured the remaining funds, and announced that all affected markets would be voided and users refunded

name: BlueMove DEX
description: BlueMove DEX's liquidity pools were drained on July 11, 2026 totaling 700K+ SUI ($500K-700K) via either an LP token double-minting mechanism introduced in a May 31 upgrade or an arithmetic overflow in the legacy AMM code. BlueMove announced shutdown and promised compensation.

name: AIDC
description: On June 28, 2026, AIDC's _sellTransfer() accumulated a 30% burn without deducting it from the seller. An attacker exploited this to withdraw from the PancakeSwap LP at inflated rates, stealing ~$121K.

name: JUDAO
description: On April 28, 2026, JUDAO was exploited on BSC via a double-sync bug in the token transfer hook that miscalculated pool balances. The attacker used a Moolah flash loan (2.3M USDT) to manipulate pricing and sell JUDAO at artificially inflated prices.

name: Sonic ICP
description: Sonic DEX, a decentralized exchange on Internet Computer, suffered an exploit involving transaction atomicity failures during asynchronous canister execution. The attacker submitted coordinated, high-frequency requests that exploited race conditions during intermediate state transitions, allowing unauthorized withdrawals before the protocol completed reconciliation. The attack affected 26 liquidity pools and resulted in approximately $276,000 in losses. Sonic paused the protocol and began implementing changes to prevent similar state inconsistencies

name: Purrlend
description: Purrlend's 2-of-3 admin multisig was compromised on HyperEVM and MegaETH, allowing attackers to assign themselves the bridge role and inherit elevated permissions to drain liquidity pools.

name: Set Protocol
description: ETHMACOAPY’s actualizeFee() rounded redemption backing upward even when no fee was payable. Attackers donated collateral to trigger recalculation, temporarily acquired Set tokens, then redeemed them for more collateral than they contributed, with the difference coming from existing holders’ backing. Two separate EOAs repeated the process across two transactions, draining approximately 8.11 WETH

name: Blend Pools V2
description: On February 22, 2026, an attacker pumped Stellar's thin USTRY market from ~$1.06 to ~$106.74, inflating collateral values. Two transactions drained $10.97M (1M USDC + 61M XLM) from YieldBlox DAO's Blend V2 lending pool, exploiting the lack of liquidity checks and anomaly detection in the oracle.

name: Binance CEX
description: On October 29, attackers exploited Binance’s operational infrastructure to execute unauthorized withdrawals across multiple blockchains, resulting in approximately $6.3 billion in losses. Binance’s preliminary investigation identified a potentially compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop that allowed access to a service container, with no evidence of wallet private key leakage. Approximately $3 billion in stolen assets were later frozen with help from industry partners. Binance committed to covering all losses using its SAFU fund and company reserves

name: Hinkal
description: Attackers exploited deprecated note format in Hinkal's shielded-pool, performing unauthorized proofless deposits and bypassing proof verification for withdrawals. Attack was isolated to Ethereum.

name: Sweat Foundation
description: On April 29, 2026, an attacker exploited a logic flaw in the SWEAT token contract on NEAR Protocol, draining 13.71B SWEAT tokens (~$3.5M) from foundation wallets within 30 seconds via a malicious drain contract. Stolen tokens were quickly liquidated via MEXC and Rhea Finance; Sweat Foundation patched the contract and restored all external user balances.

name: Mars Perps
description: On December 14, 2025, Mars Protocol's Perps market on Neutron was exploited for ~$973K via skew-based pricing arbitrage. The attacker executed the same-block arbitrage pattern 15 times, exploiting that funding rates were only applied between blocks rather than within them, eliminating downside risk.

name: Mosca
description: Mosca is an on-chain MLM/membership program where users join by depositing USDT, BUSD, or USDC for internal credits to withdraw later. The exitProgram function had incomplete state resets—only user.balance was zeroed after withdrawal but not user.balanceUSDT and user.balanceUSDC, enabling repeated withdrawals of the same funds from these alternate balance fields.

name: TMX TRIBE
description: On January 5-6, 2026, attacker exploited TMX TRIBE perpetual futures (Arbitrum/Optimism) via flawed AUM calculation ignoring USDG liabilities. Repeated mint-stake-swap loops allowed artificially inflated redemptions, draining $1.4M.

name: 42DAO
description: 42DAO's Balance Coin collapsed from $1 to $0.0012 on July 22, 2026 when attacker fed a fake low BTCB price to the oracle via the Spotter module. The oracle lacked drawdown limits and price floors, triggering liquidations of BTCB vaults at far-below-market prices.

name: WOO X
description: WOO X exchange suffered a phishing attack via a fake open-source collaboration request that lured a developer to open a malicious development tool. Attackers gained access to the development environment and executed unauthorized withdrawals across nine user accounts, draining $14M across Bitcoin, Ethereum, Arbitrum, and BSC.

name: Zilliqa
description: A buffer-copy error in the Zilliqa Ledger app's Schnorr signing code since 2019 fixed the top 64 bits of every nonce at zero. Attackers recovered private keys from ~5 on-chain signatures using lattice reduction and stole approximately 683.13M ZIL, with exploitation first spotted on July 19, 2026.

name: Polymarket International
description: On June 25, 2026, Polymarket frontend was compromised via third-party vendor, injecting malicious JavaScript that phished users into approving fraudulent token transfers, draining $3M from at least 11 wallets.

name: Step Finance
description: On January 31, 2026, Step Finance suffered a $40 million operational loss when attackers compromised executive team devices, gaining unauthorized access to treasury and fee wallet signing keys/credentials. The protocol had no smart contract vulnerabilities.

name: Peapods Finance
description: Peapods Finance's aspLONGsUSDe pod on July 8, 2025 exploited for $207K via oracle misconfiguration. Attacker manipulated the WETH/aspLONGsUSDe price to inflate collateral values. The issue was in user-created pod logic, not core contracts.

name: Pond.fun
description: Pond.fun's lead software engineer Genesis exploited privileged access to the platform's smart contracts, manipulating withdrawal functions to drain 64.8 ETH from the liquidity pools. The stolen funds were bridged to Railgun for privacy before moving to centralized exchanges. Chainalysis and Elliptic were contracted to track and prevent laundering of the stolen assets.

name: PGNLZ
description: PGNLZ's flawed burn mechanism allowed attackers to burn tokens directly from the PancakeSwap USDT-PGNLZ pool's balance without proper synchronization. This artificially reduced pool reserves, creating sharp price distortions that enabled attackers to execute reverse swaps and drain approximately $100K in USDT.

name: Nesa
description: Nesa was exploited through a Cosmos EVM vulnerability involving inconsistent balance accounting between Cosmos EVM and the Cosmos SDK. In the shared exploit mechanism documented by Cosmos Labs, delegation of locked tokens from a vesting account through the staking precompile could cause an unchecked EVM balance underflow to approximately 2^256. The resulting artificial balance could then be used to overflow a high-balance victim account, reducing the victim balance to zero while transferring its legitimate tokens to the attacker, with no net increase in token supply. Nesa has confirmed exploitation of a Cosmos EVM vulnerability but has not publicly disclosed its Nesa-side exploit transaction or victim account, so application of the exact shared mechanism to Nesa remains strongly supported but not independently demonstrated at transaction level

name: Syscoin Bridge
description: Syscoin bridge exploited via parsing inconsistency between Syscoin Core and NEVM relay. A malformed UTXO burn proof with duplicate asset commitments was accepted as valid by the relay, enabling unauthorized minting of ~5B SYS tokens.

name: ForceBridge
description: On June 2, 2025, Force Bridge (Nervos Network) was exploited via missing access controls on privileged functions. Attackers drained $3.9M across ETH and BSC (539 ETH, 898,300 USDC, 257,800 USDT, 0.79 WBTC).

name: UXLINK
description: An attacker exploited a delegatecall in UXLINK's multisig wallet to rewrite the owner set without signer approval. This enabled draining ~$11.3M in stablecoins/ETH/WBTC, seizing ~490M UXLINK tokens, and minting 1-2B more before the token crashed over 70%.

name: SBI Crypto
description: On September 24, 2025 roughly $21M in BTC, ETH, LTC, DOGE and BCH flowed out of hot wallets belonging to SBI Crypto (Japanese SBI Group's mining pool) through five instant exchangers and into Tornado Cash. ZachXBT and Cyvers linked the laundering pattern to DPRK-affiliated actors; SBI Group never publicly confirmed the incident.

name: Kelp
description: On April 18, 2026, Kelp DAO's rsETH bridge was exploited for $293 million when attackers compromised LayerZero's RPC nodes via social engineering and injected fraudulent cross-chain messages. Kelp's 1-of-1 verifier configuration created a single point of failure, affecting validation across 20 chains. The attack was attributed to Lazarus Group.

name: Mosca2
description: Mosca2's join() function was a balance multiplier due to composable logic flaws. The function attempted to top-up a member's balance but instead allowed permissionless balance inflation, enabling complete treasury drainage.

name: Limit Break Payment Processor
description: A vulnerability in Limit Break’s Payment Processor allowed an attacker to abuse users’ existing token and NFT approvals to transfer assets without a legitimate marketplace purchase. Payment Processor V2 on Ethereum was exploited first, and V3 contained the same vulnerability. Limit Break paused V3 where possible, while whitehats transferred vulnerable NFTs to safe custody because V2 could not be paused and ApeChain V3 could not immediately be paused. The same underlying approval flaw could be used in reverse against WETH approvals, resulting in 660 WETH being stolen along with other tokens before whitehats could secure it

name: BNBS
description: BNBS token on BSC was exploited via a reentrancy vulnerability where the contract failed to update state before transferring funds. The attacker invoked the vulnerable function repeatedly before completion, draining funds from the contract.

name: Fogo Foundation
description: An unknown actor compromised the Fogo Foundation and transferred 400M FOGO tokens to an attacker-controlled destination. Fogo has not disclosed the specific attack vector, affected Foundation wallet, or how authorization over the tokens was obtained. The Fogo blockchain itself was not initially compromised; the network was subsequently halted as a precaution to prevent movement of the affected tokens and upgrade the network to restrict associated addresses

name: Polycule
description: On January 13, 2026, Polycule's Telegram bot for Polymarket was hacked when the server storing user private keys was breached. The bot stored keys unencrypted on a central server with inadequate security, allowing attackers to drain $230,000 from affected users.

name: BarnBridge
description: BarnBridge suffered a governance attack on July 15, 2026 when an attacker passed a malicious proposal, replaced the SMART Yield provider contract, and drained ~$776K by exploiting pre-existing USDC approvals from 50 users.

name: XT Exchange
description: XT.com lost ~$1.7M on November 28, 2024 when the hot wallet was compromised. Attacker drained twelve token types and swapped to 461.58 ETH. The exchange halted withdrawals and said user funds were covered by 1.5x reserves.

name: WealthManagementV2
description: The attacker obtained control of WealthManagementV2’s owner privileges, suspected to have resulted from a leaked owner private key. After taking ownership, the attacker used updatePlanConfig() to set period=0 and interestMultiplier/unlockMultiplier=528,300,000. Because the privileged configuration function had no timelock or parameter bounds, the attacker could invest and immediately redeem to generate artificially inflated interest, then use a second investment to unlock and withdraw the resulting balance

name: SquidRouterModule
description: SquidRouterModule, a third-party Gnosis Safe module for Squid Router, was exploited via a verification error in executeSameChainActions(). The function accepted a publicly available constant string as proof of message security. An attacker with this fixed string could impersonate Safe wallet owners and execute arbitrary calldata to drain 86 Gnosis Safe vaults over two hours, consolidating ~$3.2M worth into DAI.

name: Litecoin
description: A zero-day in Litecoin's MWEB transaction validation allowed attackers to craft malformed transactions that non-updated nodes accepted, enabling unauthorized peg-outs. Fixed via 13-block chain reorganization.

name: NEAR Intents
description: NEAR Intents was exploited through a bug in the interaction between its Omni deposit and withdrawal infrastructure and the NEAR Intents smart contract, allowing unauthorized withdrawals. The team stopped services, patched the contract-side vulnerability, and temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals across multiple networks while completing fixes to the Omni infrastructure. The stolen funds were traced toward KuCoin and then BTC, and NEAR Intents said the losses would be compensated in full

name: Lazy Summer Protocol
description: On July 6, 2026, Summer.fi's Lazy Summer Protocol USDC vaults were exploited when an impaired Silo vault (from November 2025 Stream Finance collapse) remained in NAV calculations. The attacker accumulated vault tokens whose value hadn't reflected economic impairment, transferred them to inflate totalAssets, and redeemed at inflated price for $6.04M in genuine USDC.

name: Notional V2
description: An attacker exploited an unchecked uint128 cast in Notional V1’s collateral valuation logic. By minting two fCash positions against the same payer with notionals of 1 and 2^128-1, the attacker engineered a debt balance of exactly 2^128. When the free-collateral check converted the debt to ETH, uint128(balance.abs()) truncated 2^128 to zero, making the insolvent payer appear to have no debt. The attacker then settled the fabricated fCash claims and withdrew approximately $1.73M in USDC and DAI from the Escrow

name: Allbridge
description: Allbridge’s CCTPTokenMessenger treated a valid Circle-attested message as proof that USDC had actually been transferred. An attacker created an arbitrary CCTP message on Polygon declaring a 1,000,000 USDC transfer without burning any USDC and directed its recipient to an attacker-controlled contract rather than Circle’s TokenMessengerV2. Circle legitimately attested the generic message, but redeeming it on Base minted no USDC. Allbridge nevertheless trusted the attacker-controlled amount encoded in the message and recorded a 1,000,000 USDC deposit without checking for a corresponding token balance increase. The attacker flash-loaned 808,844 USDC to temporarily bring the router’s balance to the declared amount, redeemed the phantom credit for 999,000 USDC, repaid the loan, and drained the router’s existing liquidity. A copycat subsequently used the same technique to take the remaining funds

name: Matcha
description: Matcha Meta users lost $13.43M on January 25, 2026 when the SwapNet aggregator was exploited for arbitrary-call ability. The vulnerability allowed unauthorized access to user-approved tokens across Base and Ethereum. The frontend UI inadequately warned about approval risks.

name: Upbit
description: Upbit hot wallet was drained on November 27, 2025 in 54 minutes for $36M in Solana tokens (USDC, BONK, JTO, SONIC, RAY, RENDER, ORCA, PYTH). Attacker exploited weak digital signature infrastructure that allowed private key derivation from on-chain transaction history.

name: Verus-Ethereum Bridge
